development: The neural tube — the start of the brain and spinal cord — closes, and the placenta begins to form.
heads_up: A home test usually turns positive now. Folic acid matters most in exactly these weeks.
facts: 400 mcg of folic acid a day is what closes the neural tube, and it matters most in the weeks before most people know they are pregnant. | A home test is most reliable from the first missed day; an early negative is worth repeating in a few days.

development: The heart tube starts to beat, and the buds that become arms and legs appear.
heads_up: Book a first prenatal visit — most practices see you around week 8.
facts: Call to book the first prenatal visit — most practices see you between 8 and 10 weeks. | Nausea often starts now. Small, dry, frequent snacks work better than trying to eat a meal.

development: Facial features, eyes and the inner ear begin to take shape.
heads_up: Nausea and fatigue often start here and are usually worst between weeks 6 and 12.
facts: An early scan can usually find a heartbeat from about now. | Caffeine under 200 mg a day — roughly one 12 oz coffee — is the usual guidance.

development: Brain cells multiply quickly and the hands and feet emerge as paddles.
heads_up: Sickness can come at any hour — small, frequent snacks tend to help more than big meals.
facts: No amount of alcohol has been shown to be safe in pregnancy, so the advice is none. | Keep the prenatal vitamin going on the sick days too; iron and iodine are the parts that matter most.

development: Fingers and toes separate and every major organ is under construction.
heads_up: First prenatal appointment: bloodwork, a dating scan and a confirmed due date.
facts: First visit is usually around now: bloods, blood type and Rh, and a dating scan. | A flu shot is recommended in any trimester and passes antibodies to the baby.

development: Joints bend, and the heartbeat can often be heard on ultrasound.
heads_up: Ask about prenatal screening options — many are offered from week 10.
facts: Nausea usually peaks this week and eases through the end of the first trimester. | NIPT (cell-free DNA screening) can be drawn from 10 weeks — ask now if you want it.

development: Officially a fetus now — the vital organs are formed and starting to work.
heads_up: Cell-free DNA screening is available from about now and can also report sex.
facts: Gums bleed more easily in pregnancy. Dental cleaning is safe and worth booking. | NIPT reports chromosomal risk, and fetal sex as a by-product.

development: Fingernails appear and the fetus moves constantly, though you cannot feel it yet.
heads_up: Energy may still be low. It is a demanding trimester even when nothing shows.
facts: The nuchal translucency scan runs between 11 and 14 weeks. | Once a heartbeat is seen at this stage, the chance of miscarriage falls sharply.

development: Reflexes develop and the fetus can open and close its hands.
heads_up: The nuchal translucency scan window is weeks 11–14. Miscarriage risk drops sharply after this point.
facts: Energy usually starts coming back over the next few weeks. | This is where most people share the news, for the reason above.

development: Vocal cords form and the fetus begins practising breathing motions with amniotic fluid.
heads_up: Second trimester begins — nausea often eases and appetite returns.
facts: Second trimester — for most people the steadiest stretch of the three. | Start sleeping on your side from now. Left is often suggested; either side is fine.

development: Facial muscles work: squinting, frowning, grimacing. Fine lanugo hair covers the body.
heads_up: A good stretch for travel if you want any.
facts: A sharp pull low in the abdomen when you move is round ligament pain, and it is harmless. | 150 minutes of moderate activity a week is the standard target unless your provider has said otherwise.

development: Bones harden and the fetus can sense light through closed eyelids.
heads_up: You may start to show. Side-sleeping gets more comfortable than lying on your back.
facts: Quad screen bloods run 15–22 weeks where they are offered. | Amniocentesis, where it is indicated, is done from 15 weeks.

development: The head is upright and the heart pumps around 25 quarts of blood a day.
heads_up: Second-trimester bloodwork is usually offered between 15 and 20 weeks.
facts: First movements arrive between 16 and 22 weeks — later if the placenta is at the front. | Blood volume is up by nearly half by now, so standing up fast will make you dizzy.

development: Fat stores begin forming and the umbilical cord thickens.
heads_up: Round-ligament twinges are common as the uterus grows.
facts: Book the anatomy scan if you have not: it runs 18–22 weeks. | Heartburn starts for many. Smaller meals and staying upright afterwards do more than anything else.

development: Hearing sharpens — voices and heartbeats register. Myelin starts coating the nerves.
heads_up: Talk and read out loud. Familiar voices are recognisable at birth.
facts: The anatomy scan checks organs, growth and where the placenta is sitting. Allow 45 minutes or more. | Hearing is working — newborns show a preference for voices they heard before birth.

development: Vernix, a waxy coating, forms to protect the skin against the amniotic fluid.
heads_up: The anatomy scan is usually 18–22 weeks and sex is often visible there.
facts: Night leg cramps are common now; stretching the calf before bed helps. | Ask about a glucose test date — it runs 24–28 weeks.

development: Halfway. The fetus swallows regularly and starts producing meconium.
heads_up: Measurements switch from crown-to-rump to head-to-heel this week — that is why the length jumps.
facts: Halfway. Fundal height in centimetres roughly tracks the week from about now. | If you are having a baby shower or leave conversation, this is the comfortable window for it.

development: Movements become the coordinated kicks you can start to feel.
heads_up: First flutters usually land somewhere between weeks 18 and 22.
facts: The baby swallows amniotic fluid and tastes what you eat; that exposure shapes later food acceptance. | Movements are still irregular — patterns come later.

development: Lips, eyelids and eyebrows are distinct, and the sense of touch develops.
heads_up: Glucose screening is usually scheduled for weeks 24–28.
facts: Vernix and fine lanugo hair cover the skin. | Start a hospital bag list now; packing it can wait until about 33 weeks.

development: Blood vessels in the lungs develop in preparation for breathing air.
heads_up: Around the viability threshold — outcomes improve week by week from here with neonatal care.
facts: Survival rates climb steeply across these few weeks with neonatal care. | Know the signs of preterm labour: regular tightening, low backache, pressure, any fluid or bleeding. Call, do not wait.

development: Lungs start making surfactant, the substance that keeps the air sacs open.
heads_up: Glucose tolerance window opens. Worth asking what preterm labor feels like.
facts: The glucose tolerance test runs 24–28 weeks. | If you have preterm risk factors, ask whether cervical length monitoring applies to you.

development: Fat fills out the skin and hair takes on colour and texture.
heads_up: Baby responds to your voice — you may feel a kick when you talk.
facts: Swollen feet at the end of the day are ordinary. Sudden swelling of the face and hands with a headache is not — call the same day. | Third-trimester iron needs climb; anaemia screening is usually repeated around now.

development: Eyes open for the first time and the startle reflex appears.
heads_up: Consider a hospital tour and a childbirth class if you want them.
facts: The baby now responds to sound with movement, and sleep cycles have begun. | Heartburn and breathlessness build from here. Extra pillows, smaller meals.

development: Regular sleep and wake cycles begin, with recognisable breathing motions.
heads_up: Last week of the second trimester. Movement patterns start to be worth noticing.
facts: Tdap is recommended in every pregnancy between 27 and 36 weeks — the antibodies cross over and protect against whooping cough in the months before the baby can be vaccinated. | Visits usually move to every two weeks around now.

development: The brain surface folds and grooves and blinking begins.
heads_up: Visits usually move to every two weeks. Rh-negative parents get an injection around now.
facts: Start counting movements daily: ten movements inside two hours is the usual reassurance. Any change from the baby's own pattern is a same-day call. | Anti-D is given about now if you are Rh negative.

development: Bones are fully formed but still soft while muscles and lungs keep maturing.
heads_up: Daily movement counts are a simple way to notice change — call about any decrease.
facts: Colostrum may start leaking. It means nothing about later supply either way. | Book the car seat fitting — many fire stations and hospitals check them free.

development: Bone marrow takes over red blood cell production and lanugo starts to shed.
heads_up: Heartburn and shortness of breath are common as space runs short.
facts: Braxton Hicks tightenings get more noticeable. Regular and painful is not Braxton Hicks — call. | Ten weeks out is a good point to sort parental leave paperwork.

development: All five senses work and the fetus can turn its head toward light.
heads_up: Braxton Hicks tightenings are normal. Regular painful ones are not — call.
facts: The baby is putting on roughly half a pound a week from here. | Practise the route to the hospital at the time of day you would actually be travelling.

development: Practice breathing is near constant and toenails and real hair are in.
heads_up: Most babies settle head-down around now. A breech position often still turns.
facts: Most babies turn head-down between 32 and 36 weeks. | Pack the bag this month: ID, notes, phone charger, going-home clothes for both of you.

development: The immune system takes on antibodies passed across the placenta.
heads_up: Pack a hospital bag this month — birth from 34 weeks is not unusual.
facts: Write down the birth preferences you genuinely care about — one page is plenty. | Sleep is broken from here; nap when you can rather than saving it up.

development: Lungs are nearly ready. A baby born now is late preterm, and usually does well.
heads_up: Group B strep swab is usually done at 36 weeks.
facts: From 34 weeks a baby is late preterm: usually fine, but sleepier at the breast and more prone to jaundice. | Confirm who is coming to the birth and who is on call for the drive.

development: Weight gain accelerates to roughly half a pound a week from here.
heads_up: Visits usually become weekly. Confirm the route and any childcare plans.
facts: The group B strep swab runs 36–37 weeks and decides whether you are offered antibiotics in labour. | Choose the baby's pediatrician now — the first visit is 2–3 days after you get home.

development: The digestive system is complete and the skull stays soft to ease the passage out.
heads_up: Early term starts at 37 weeks. Learn the signs of labor now.
facts: Visits go weekly from about now. | Install the car seat and have it checked: rear-facing, harness at or below the shoulders, no bulky coats underneath.

development: Early term. The brain and lungs keep maturing right through week 39.
heads_up: Every extra week before 39 measurably helps feeding and breathing.
facts: Early term. Elective delivery before 39 weeks is avoided without a medical reason — the last weeks add real brain and lung development. | Know when to go in: regular contractions, waters breaking, bleeding, or reduced movements.

development: Fat continues to build and the grip is firm.
heads_up: Watch for waters breaking, and for contractions getting longer, stronger and closer together.
facts: Everything from here is a waiting game that ends on its own. | Batch-cook or stock the freezer this week if you have the energy.

development: Full term. Brain growth stays rapid right up to birth.
heads_up: Losing the mucus plug can happen days or hours before labor.
facts: Full term. This is the window with the best outcomes for an uncomplicated pregnancy. | Rest rather than walking yourself into exhaustion trying to start labour.

development: Ready. Most babies arrive within a week either side of this date.
heads_up: Only about one baby in twenty arrives on the due date. Later is normal.
facts: Only about one baby in twenty arrives on the due date; 37–42 weeks is all ordinary. | Monitoring usually steps up from here rather than anything being wrong.

development: Late term. The placenta keeps working, and is monitored more closely now.
heads_up: Expect extra monitoring and a conversation about induction around weeks 41–42.
facts: Late term. Checks typically move to twice weekly, and induction is usually offered by 41–42 weeks. | Ask what your provider's plan and timeline actually are, so the decision is not made in a rush.
